introduction-the-physics-of-resistance.core: Good ideas fail because change is emotional and social, not just technical. People lose familiar competence, routines and status, so even beneficial changes meet resistance that has to be managed.

first_principles.problem: A tool that saves 50% of effort is rejected because the rollout ignored how people feel about changing.
derivation: Expect the **emotional dip** (Satir).
Follow a **leadership roadmap** (Kotter).
**Sustain** the change after launch.
**Combine** the models.

analogy.title: Inertia in physics
analogy.story: Objects at rest stay at rest unless a force acts on them, and organisations behave the same way.
analogy.breaks: Not all resistance is irrational. Some of it flags real flaws in the change.

example.title: The perfect tool, rejected

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: The rollout, not the tool, failed.

example.outcome: change treated as a human process.

check.q: Why do technically superior changes still fail?
check.a: They ignore the human side of change: lost competence, routines and identity, plus the temporary performance dip.

the-satir-change-model-predicting-the-em.core: Satir's model: Late Status Quo → a Foreign Element (the change) → Chaos (performance drops, frustration) → a Transforming Idea (people see how to make it work) → Practice and Integration → a New Status Quo at a higher level. The dip is normal.

first_principles.problem: Leaders panic at the productivity dip after a change and roll back just before the improvement would arrive.
truths: Learning new ways temporarily lowers performance.
Emotions are strongest in the chaos phase.
derivation: **Predict** the dip and communicate it upfront.
**Support** during chaos: training, pairing, office hours.
**Celebrate** transforming ideas (early wins).
**Don't abort** during the predictable trough.

analogy.title: Learning a new keyboard layout
analogy.story: You type slower for weeks before you become faster than ever.
analogy.breaks: Some changes genuinely fail, so distinguish the expected dip from real problems with data.

example.title: A monorepo migration

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Leadership holds steady through the dip.

example.outcome: you can predict and manage the emotional curve.

check.a: Performance and morale drop as people struggle with the new way before mastering it.

kotters-8-steps-a-roadmap-for-leaders.core: Kotter's first phases set up change: (1) create urgency, (2) form a guiding coalition, (3) build a vision and strategy, (4) communicate the vision, (5) remove obstacles, (6) generate short-term wins. Skipping steps is the most common reason transformations fail.

first_principles.problem: Leaders announce a vision with no urgency or coalition, and the change fizzles out.
truths: People need a reason to change.
No one person can drive large change.
derivation: **Urgency**: show the cost of the status quo with data.
**Coalition**: respected people from across the org.
**Vision** and constant **communication**.
**Remove obstacles** (tools, policies) and **deliver early wins**.

analogy.title: Organising a community clean-up
analogy.story: Show the problem (litter photos), recruit respected neighbours, share a clear plan, provide bins and gloves, and celebrate the first clean street.
analogy.breaks: It's a linear model applied to messy reality, so use it as a checklist, not a rigid sequence.

example.title: Driving SLO adoption
flow: Vision: every service has SLOs by Q4
Remove obstacles: SLO templates in platform
example.outcome: change led with a proven roadmap.

check.q: Why does Kotter emphasise creating urgency first?
check.a: Without a compelling reason to change, people default to the status quo.

kotters-phase-3-sticking-the-landing.core: Kotter's final steps: (7) build on the change (don't declare victory too soon; use credibility to change more) and (8) anchor it in culture (embed it in processes, hiring, onboarding and norms), so the change survives once the champions move on.

first_principles.problem: After launch excitement fades, teams quietly revert to old ways, and the transformation dies.
truths: New behaviours are fragile at first.
derivation: **Keep going** after the first wins: tackle the next obstacles.
**Measure** adoption and outcomes continuously.
**Embed** into onboarding, templates, CI checks and promotion criteria.
**Retire** the old way explicitly.

analogy.title: Planting a tree
analogy.story: It needs staking and watering until its roots are deep enough to stand alone.
analogy.breaks: Over-entrenching a change makes the next change harder, so leave room to evolve.

check.q: What does 'anchoring the change in culture' involve?
check.a: Embedding new practices into processes, templates, onboarding and norms so they persist independently.

combining-the-models-a-unified-mental-ma.core: Kotter tells leaders what to do (the organisational process). Satir explains what people feel along the way. Together: run Kotter's steps while anticipating and supporting people through Satir's chaos, timing early wins to lift them out of the dip.

first_principles.problem: Leaders follow a process checklist but ignore emotions, or empathise but lack a plan.
truths: Early wins help people through the chaos.
Support reduces the depth of the dip.
derivation: Map **Kotter steps onto the Satir curve**.
Put **urgency and vision** before the foreign element.
Offer **support and obstacle removal** during chaos.
Make **short-term wins** the transforming idea; **anchor** in the new status quo.

analogy.title: A guided mountain hike
analogy.story: The route plan (Kotter) and the guide reading the group's energy (Satir) together get everyone to the summit.
analogy.breaks: Real change is iterative, with several overlapping curves for different groups.

example.title: Planning a migration with both models
flow: Launch: expect chaos; open office hours
Month 3: embed in templates, retire old tool

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A shorter dip and lasting adoption.

example.outcome: change led with both process and empathy.

check.q: How do Kotter's short-term wins relate to Satir's model?
check.a: They act as the 'transforming idea' that lifts people out of the chaos phase.
